Informed Consent in Research

Principles, Law & Practice — an interactive module with video lectures, case studies, flashcards and a final assessment.

params.alt: BriGRETE title slide: Informed Consent — Bridging the Gap in Research Ethics Training & Education.
Diagram defining informed consent through autonomy, self-determination and human dignity, with the note that consent is more than signing a form.

params.text:
What Informed Consent Means

Informed consent is the structural cornerstone of any research project that involves human participants. It is grounded in three linked principles: autonomy, self-determination and respect for human dignity. At its heart, it is the bridge that balances the drive for scientific progress against the absolute duty to protect the people who make that progress possible.

Crucially, consent is far more than a signature on a designated form. It is an ongoing, transparent confirmation that a person genuinely understands a study and freely agrees to take part. That agreement only carries ethical and legal weight once the participant has received a comprehensive disclosure of every fact relevant to their decision — the purpose of the study, how it will run, its risks and benefits, and the alternatives open to them.

Done well, this process builds trust, respects each person's right to decide what happens to their own body and data, and helps researchers uphold the ethical standards their work depends on.

Watch: The Architecture of Autonomy

This short lecture walks through the full arc of informed consent — from its historical foundations to the modern consent document. Captions are available: click the CC button in the player to turn the transcript on.

params.text:
Who This Module Is For

This module is designed for two broad groups working across the research landscape:

  • Research Ethics Committee (REC) members — both new members who want structured, foundational training, and experienced members deepening their grasp of specialised areas such as AI ethics and digital data ethics.
  • Researchers — early-career researchers (postgraduate students, PhD candidates and postdoctoral researchers) who need solid foundations, and mid-career or senior researchers engaging with advanced issues in AI, data management and interdisciplinary work.

params.alt: Balance scale weighing the pursuit of knowledge against the protection of human dignity, labelled an ethical and legal obligation.
List of five key learning objectives: understand, recognize, apply, interpret and design.

params.text:
Purpose & Learning Objectives

In today's diverse and complex research environment, informed consent is both an ethical and a legal obligation, balancing the pursuit of knowledge with the protection of human dignity. This module equips you with practical knowledge and tools to run a streamlined, respectful consent process.

By the end of the module, you will be able to:

  • Understand the core ethical principles of informed consent — autonomy, voluntariness and respect for persons.
  • Recognise and describe the essential elements of consent, such as disclosure, comprehension and voluntariness.
  • Apply consent principles in diverse contexts, including with vulnerable populations and complex protocols.
  • Interpret international and national frameworks such as the Belmont Report, the Declaration of Helsinki, the Clinical Trials Regulation and the GDPR.
  • Design consent processes that ensure clear communication, cultural sensitivity and participant empowerment.

params.text:
Communication, Not Paperwork

Informed consent is best understood as open and honest communication between researchers and participants, not a one-off administrative step. It rests on three connected pillars:

  • Clear information — participants receive a plain-language account of the study's purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives.
  • Building trust — honest dialogue reassures people that their rights and wellbeing come first, and helps them see how their contribution advances science and the wider good.
  • Voluntary choice — the decision to take part is entirely the participant's own, free from pressure, coercion or undue influence.

Because circumstances and understanding can change, consent is treated as continuous and revisitable — participants may ask questions, seek reassurance, or withdraw at any point.

params.text:
How Modern Consent Rules Were Forged

The strict consent frameworks we rely on today did not appear by design — they were a direct response to grave abuses. Three landmark texts turned the abstract philosophy of human rights into actionable, internationally recognised protocols for research.

params.alt: History slide on the 1947 Nuremberg Code: a response to WWII atrocities, establishing the need for voluntary agreement and ten core principles.
Evolution slide on the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki: twelve principles, the distinction between care and research, surrogate consent and written documentation.
Belmont Report triangle showing respect for persons, beneficence and justice, dated 1979, U.S. National Commission.

params.text: Conceived after the Nuremberg trials, in response to cruel experiments performed by Nazi doctors on prisoners who had not consented, the Code was the first international document on research ethics. It set out ten principles and made voluntary, uncoerced, fully informed consent the absolute baseline for any research involving people.

Adopted by the 18th World Medical Assembly and revised many times since, Helsinki addressed gaps the Nuremberg Code left open. Its twelve principles stressed the primacy of patient welfare, ethics-committee approval, the right to withdraw and transparency. It distinguished medical care that benefits the patient from research that may not, introduced surrogate (proxy) consent by a legal guardian for those unable to consent, and required that consent be documented in writing.

Published by the U.S. National Commission, the Belmont Report established three foundational principles: respect for persons (honouring autonomy and protecting those with diminished autonomy), beneficence (maximising benefits while minimising harm), and justice (the fair distribution of the benefits and burdens of research). It also shaped the framework for Institutional Review Boards.

params.title: Review the history and the Belmont principles.

dialogs.answer: Cruel and unethical medical experiments performed by Nazi doctors during World War II.

dialogs.text: How many core principles were promulgated in the final court decision known as the Nuremberg Code?
dialogs.answer: Ten principles.

dialogs.text: What was the Nuremberg Code's primary mechanism for ensuring voluntary participation?
dialogs.answer: Informed consent provided with full knowledge of the research implications.

dialogs.text: In 1964, the 18th World Medical Assembly adopted which major document on biomedical research ethics?
dialogs.answer: The Declaration of Helsinki.

dialogs.text: How many principles were originally adopted in the Declaration of Helsinki to guide physicians?
dialogs.answer: Twelve principles.

dialogs.text: What distinction did the Declaration of Helsinki stress regarding medical interventions?
dialogs.answer: The difference between medical care that directly benefits the patient and research which may not.

dialogs.text: Who is authorized to give consent under the Declaration of Helsinki if a subject is legally incapable?
dialogs.answer: A legal guardian acting on their behalf.

dialogs.text: Which document introduced the specific requirement that consent must be documented in writing?
dialogs.answer: The Declaration of Helsinki.

dialogs.text: What are the three basic ethical principles established by the Belmont Report (1979)?
dialogs.answer: Respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

dialogs.text: How does the Belmont Report define the principle of 'Respect for Persons'?
dialogs.answer: Recognizing individual autonomy and protecting those with diminished autonomy.

dialogs.text: What is the primary obligation of the 'Beneficence' principle in the Belmont Report?
dialogs.answer: Maximizing potential benefits while minimizing potential risks of harm.

dialogs.text: How is the principle of 'Justice' defined within the framework of the Belmont Report?
dialogs.answer: The fair distribution of the benefits and burdens of research.

params.text:
Binding International Instruments

Beyond the foundational declarations, two instruments give informed consent firm legal force in Europe.

The Oviedo Convention (1997)

Issued by the Council of Europe, the Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine is the first legally binding international treaty protecting human rights in biomedicine. It treats consent as a keystone of practice and research: under Article 5, no medical intervention may take place without the voluntary and informed agreement of the person concerned. For research, Article 16 requires that participants be informed of their rights and legal safeguards. Consent must be given expressly and specifically, be documented, and may be freely withdrawn at any time. Projects must also be approved by a competent body — an Ethics Committee or Institutional Review Board — after independent, multidisciplinary review of their scientific merit and ethical acceptability.

The Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014

For clinical trials on medicinal products, Article 29 requires informed consent to be written, dated and signed by both the person conducting the interview and the participant (or their legally designated representative). An information letter must cover the trial's purpose, risks, benefits, alternatives and the participant's rights, including the right to withdraw. Consent must be freely and voluntarily given, documented in writing, and the participant must receive a copy.

params.alt: Slide on GDPR and data protection, referencing Article 6(1) as a basis for processing personal data in research.

params.text:
A Separate Legal Requirement

Informed consent under research ethics and informed consent under data-protection law are two distinct things. Even when a researcher complies with the Oviedo Convention or the Clinical Trials Regulation, they must still satisfy the GDPR when collecting and processing personal data. Recital 161 makes clear that consent to participate in a trial does not replace the obligation, under Article 6 GDPR, to identify an appropriate lawful basis for processing personal data.

Where consent is the chosen lawful basis, Article 4(11) defines it as any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes, given by a statement or a clear affirmative action. Article 7 adds that the controller must be able to prove consent was obtained, and that the data subject may withdraw it at any time.

Data subjects must receive enough information to make a real choice — including the identity of the data controller, the categories of data processed, the purposes of processing, the recipients, the storage period, their rights, and the consequences of not consenting.

Consent must relate to the particular purpose and consequences of processing. It cannot cover undefined or open-ended activities — vaguely referring to 'research relating to an epidemic study', for example, is not valid.
Participants must be able to consent or refuse without harm, and to withdraw at any time. Consent must not be bundled with, or made contingent on, unrelated terms and conditions.

params.title: Review the GDPR rules on consent.

dialogs.text: Under Article 6(1) of the GDPR, what role does informed consent play in data processing?
dialogs.answer: It serves as one of the legitimation grounds for lawful data processing.

dialogs.text: Does consent to participate in a clinical trial automatically satisfy GDPR requirements for data processing?
dialogs.answer: No, it is an entirely separate requirement that does not outweigh the obligation to identify a lawful basis under GDPR.

dialogs.text: How does Article 4 lit. 11 of the GDPR define 'consent'?
dialogs.answer: A freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes.

dialogs.text: According to Article 7 of the GDPR, what right does a data subject have regarding their consent?
dialogs.answer: The right to withdraw consent at any time.

dialogs.text: To be considered 'informed' under the GDPR, what must a data subject know about the data controller?
dialogs.answer: The specific identity of the data controller.

dialogs.text: Under the GDPR, what does the requirement for 'specific' consent entail?
dialogs.answer: Consent must relate to the precise purpose and consequences of processing rather than undefined activities.

dialogs.text: Under what condition is consent considered 'freely given' according to the GDPR?
dialogs.answer: When the subject can refuse or withdraw without harm and consent is not contingent on other terms.

dialogs.text: What power dynamics should researchers address to ensure consent for data processing is truly freely given?
dialogs.answer: Factual or legal hierarchies and economic dependencies between the researcher and participant.

dialogs.text: Why is 'plain and clear language' required in research information sheets?
dialogs.answer: To allow participants to make an informed decision on whether to participate.

params.alt: Slide on navigating special circumstances: power dynamics, vulnerable populations, cultural norms and observational studies.

params.text:
When Standard Consent Is Not Enough

For consent to data processing to be truly freely given, researchers must address the realities of the situation:

  • Power dynamics — factual or legal hierarchies and economic dependencies between researcher and participant can quietly undermine voluntariness.
  • Vulnerability — the susceptibility of the population being studied calls for extra safeguards.
  • Impact of findings — researchers must ensure results do not stigmatise or expose individuals and communities to discrimination.

Several special situations call for tailored approaches: where written consent clashes with cultural or ethical norms, use alternatives such as oral consent with witnesses and document everything; for those unable to consent, apply equivalent protective measures and seek consent from a legal representative or parent; in observational studies, secure gatekeeper approval beforehand, or consent afterward where identities are anonymised. Public observation may not require consent if privacy is respected and behaviour is unaffected. Consent given by family members or employers can never substitute for an individual's own consent.

params.title: Review how to handle special circumstances.

dialogs.answer: When written consent is unsuitable due to specific cultural or ethical norms.

dialogs.text: When might public observations in research *not* require individual consent?
dialogs.answer: If privacy is respected and behavior remains unaffected by the observation.

params.alt: IRB review process slide: review plan, assess treatment, balance risks and benefits, as mandatory oversight before a study begins.

params.text:
From Proposal to Approval

The consent process begins long before anyone signs a form — it starts with a research proposal that states the study's context and objectives up front. Before the study can begin, the plan must pass a mandatory checkpoint: review by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Ethics Committee.

The board's duty is to ensure research is conducted ethically and that participants' rights, safety and privacy are protected. It checks whether: participants are treated fairly and with respect; they will genuinely understand the study and its risks through a clear consent process; and the potential risks are justified by the possible benefits. Acting as an independent firewall, the board ensures no study reaches human subjects without external, objective proof of its ethical soundness.

dialogs.answer: The possible benefits of the research.

params.alt: First half of the elements of written consent: study overview, purpose, procedures, risks, benefits and alternatives.
Second half of the elements of written consent: confidentiality, risk compensation, remuneration, contact information and voluntary participation.

params.text:
The Eleven Mandatory Components

Once a project is approved, the plan is translated into a written informed consent document. It should open with the key information a participant needs to understand the study's purpose, and is built from eleven mandatory elements. Expand each below.
A clear statement that the activity involves research.
The research purpose and the expected time commitment for participants.
A description of all procedures, including those that are experimental.
Potential risks or discomforts, their likelihood, and the measures taken to reduce them.
Any expected benefits for the participant or others — excluding monetary compensation.
Disclosure of alternative treatments or procedures that might benefit the participant.
How participant records will be kept confidential and who may access them.
For more-than-minimal-risk studies: compensation, medical treatment for injuries, and contacts for further information.
Any compensation offered to participants.
Whom to contact with questions about the research, participant rights, or related concerns.
Assurance that participation is voluntary, with no penalty or loss of benefits for refusing or withdrawing at any time.

An exception to using a written consent form can be requested when a form is impractical or detrimental to the study — for example, observation of public behaviour, emergency situations, research with certain vulnerable populations, or the use of pre-existing data or samples — but only with careful justification and approval from the appropriate ethics body.

params.alt: Slide contrasting acceptable practices with prohibited practices for ensuring true voluntariness in consent.

params.text:
Free From Pressure

Throughout the process, the participant — or their legal proxy — must remain free from any manipulation or pressure from researchers, sponsors or medical staff. Some practices are firmly prohibited: obtaining consent through deception or misinformation, creating a sense of obligation, or making participation forced or threatened. The acceptable standard is that information has been adequately discussed and clarified before consent is freely given.

Valid consent must be secured before any non-standard medical tests or trial-specific evaluations are carried out. The framework culminates in the participant personally signing and dating the document — physical proof that a transparent dialogue took place, that the person made an informed choice, and that the community's ethical standards were met.

params.title: Review acceptable and prohibited practices.

dialogs.text: Prohibited Practice: Manipulation
dialogs.answer: Obtaining consent through deception or misinformation.

dialogs.text: Prohibited Practice: Pressure/Obligation
dialogs.answer: Creating a situation where the participant feels duty-bound or constrained to agree.

dialogs.text: Prohibited Practice: Forced Participation
dialogs.answer: Making participation mandatory or placing it under threat.

dialogs.text: Acceptable Practice: Adequately Discussed
dialogs.answer: Ensuring information is thoroughly understood and clarified before consent.

params.alt: Case study slide: the scenario of Dr Maria Collins, covering vulnerability and trust, informed consent and cultural sensitivity, the need to report, and risk-benefit balance.
Ethical response slide for the privacy breach, with steps and discussion questions.

panels.title: Case 1 — The data breach (Dr Maria Collins)

params.text: Dr Collins studies mental-health outcomes among survivors of domestic violence, promising complete confidentiality and anonymity. A breach of her secure database exposes sensitive, anonymised profiles — creating a serious risk of re-identification. Although no names were taken directly, the promise underpinning participants' trust has been threatened, and they have a right to know.

The response must be structural: run an immediate security audit and upgrade systems; provide professional counselling, since exposure could cause real distress; and re-contact every participant to update their consent and offer them the chance to withdraw. Notification and transparency come first.

The same breach raises sharper questions for marginalised participants, who may fear their data could be used against them. It highlights the need for culturally sensitive communication, consent processes that spell out the limits of anonymity, and institutional guidelines for research with vulnerable communities.

params.alt: Case study slide on posthumous use of biological material: the scenario of Georgina Pond and the violation of autonomy.
Ethical response slide for the posthumous-use case, with steps and discussion questions.

panels.title: Case 3 — Posthumous use without consent (Georgina Pond)

params.text: Doctors extract stem cells from a hospitalised patient, Georgina Pond, without informing her or her family. After she dies, the cells fuel a major breakthrough for treating Parkinson's disease. The lead researcher, Dr Robinson, now faces a collision between beneficence (a life-saving discovery) and a severe violation of autonomy (material taken without permission).

A successful outcome does not retroactively erase the violation. Dr Robinson must acknowledge the breach, audit her team's practices to find where oversight failed, report to a competent Research Ethics Committee, and communicate the benefits to society without minimising or hiding the original failure to obtain consent. She should also engage the family honestly and consider appropriate redress.

dialogs.text: What three core principles ground the concept of informed consent in research?

dialogs.text: What was the historical catalyst for the creation of the Nuremberg Code in 1947?
dialogs.answer: Cruel and unethical medical experiments performed by Nazi doctors during World War II.

dialogs.text: In 1964, the 18th World Medical Assembly adopted which major document on biomedical research ethics?
dialogs.answer: The Declaration of Helsinki.

dialogs.text: What are the three basic ethical principles established by the Belmont Report (1979)?
dialogs.answer: Respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

dialogs.text: Which 1997 treaty was the first legally binding international document for human rights in biomedicine?
dialogs.answer: The Oviedo Convention.

dialogs.text: Regarding clinical trials for medicinal products, which EU Regulation provides specific rules for informed consent?
dialogs.answer: Regulation No 536/2014.

dialogs.text: How does Article 4 lit. 11 of the GDPR define 'consent'?
dialogs.answer: A freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes.

dialogs.text: Under what condition is consent considered 'freely given' according to the GDPR?
dialogs.answer: When the subject can refuse or withdraw without harm and consent is not contingent on other terms.

dialogs.text: What is the primary duty of an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Ethics Committee?
dialogs.answer: To ensure research respects ethics and protects the rights, safety, and privacy of participants.

dialogs.text: Written Consent Element: Study Overview
dialogs.answer: A clear statement that the study involves research.

dialogs.text: Prohibited Practice: Manipulation
dialogs.answer: Obtaining consent through deception or misinformation.

dialogs.text: In the case of Dr. Maria Collins, why did a secure database breach raise issues regarding informed consent?
dialogs.answer: The leakage threatened promised confidentiality, which is a right participants must know about to stay informed.

params.text:
Key Takeaways

  • Informed consent is the cornerstone of ethical research — an ongoing, transparent dialogue grounded in autonomy, self-determination and human dignity, not merely a signature.
  • Today's rules grew from the Nuremberg Code, the Declaration of Helsinki and the Belmont Report, which together established voluntary consent, written documentation, proxy consent and the three principles of respect, beneficence and justice.
  • Binding instruments — the Oviedo Convention and the Clinical Trials Regulation — give consent legal force and require independent ethics review.
  • The GDPR treats consent to process data as a separate requirement that must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, with a right to withdraw at any time.
  • A written consent document is built from eleven elements, secured before any research-specific procedures, and finalised by a personal, dated signature given free from pressure.
  • When something goes wrong, the ethical response is transparency first: notify those affected, strengthen oversight, provide support, and honour the right to withdraw.

You now have the knowledge and tools to design and run a consent process that respects participants, satisfies the law, and strengthens the integrity of your research. Well done on completing the module.

Key Texts & Frameworks

  • Mandal J, Parija SC. Informed consent and research. Trop Parasitol. 2014;4(2):78–9.
  • Manti S, Licari A. How to obtain informed consent for research. Breathe, 2018.
  • Aniaka O. History and Importance of Informed Consent in Health Care. SSRN, 2013.
  • WMA. Declaration of Helsinki — Ethical Principles for Medical Research Involving Human Participants (1964, last amended 2024).
  • U.S. DHHS. The Belmont Report (1979).
  • Nijhawan LP et al. Informed consent: Issues and challenges. J Adv Pharm Technol Res. 2013;4(3):134–40.
  • Council of Europe. Convention on Human Rights and Biomedicine (Oviedo Convention), ETS No. 164, 1997.
  • Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 on clinical trials on medicinal products for human use.
  • European University Institute. Guide on Good Data Protection Practice in Research, 2020.
  • CIOMS. International Ethical Guidelines for Health-related Research Involving Humans, 2016.
